TextEquiv.Unicode: 986 2 January 1802
MARTHA MCTIER, [BELFAST], TO WILLIAM DRENNAN, [DUBLIN] [952]
Dear William, Cleaning, settling, paying and receiving little matters have employed
me so much since I came to town that I chose rather, daily to expect a letter, than
write one. Orr” at length arrived, brought me Sarah's,” and a cap, for which I beg she
will thank Mrs Hincks," assure her I admire it very much, and that comparatively it
is cheap. Orr is set quite on his own legs here as to acquaintances and I think he may
turn them to advantage professionally. He supped at James Kennedy's’ (hospital it
may be called) the night he came, at Mrs Crombie’s® the one after, dined at William
Sinclaire’s’ on Thursday, at Seeds’s® yesterday, at Dr Haliday’s’ today — this for his
mother." Yours" has not appeared so well (sitting) for years. She took shelter in her
snug room before she got cold and hitherto has had none.
I suppose you have heard all the particulars of poor Kennedy's” death. His was a
life of sobriety and health for fifty-five years, and one would have made choice of it
in a lease. He has left ten sons and three daughters, all of whom were in everything
educated strictly at home and ever regarded him in the light of a severe schoolmaster,
and till now were never at home without father or mother mounting guard, as they
termed it. Sober, handsome, good managers, their parents thought them wonders —
while an invincible love for fun, and ridicule, and consequently lying, has rendered
them thoroughly contemptible to the world, where their word, or story goes for
nothing. When Lord Castlereagh® their relation was here, he, his lady, and a party
went a boating, and ordered their carriages to come for them near Cultra. One of
these chaps assured the servant they were to land at Bangor, where they were in vain
waited for, while her ladyship and the rest footed it to Belfast — for which she
appears very able. The next thing they got the credit of was a pompous account in
the paper of the celebration of peace at the hospitable mansion of Florida," where
the gates were made to fly open and the tenantry treated with fruit and punch.
1 The numbers following the address are those given to the letters by the Public Record Office of Northern
Ireland as part of the series D/591; for example, this letter is numbered D/591/952.
2 Robert Orr (1770-1817), barrister, who became a close friend of Drennan’s.
3 William Drennan’s wife Sarah Swanwick (1770-1870).
4 Susan (1769-1849), wife of William Hincks, Dublin merchant, and sister of Sarah Drennan.
5 James Trail Kennedy (1751-1832), a prosperous wine and spirit merchant, and a boyhood friend of
Drennan’s; all but one of his children suffered protracted illnesses and died young.
6 Elizabeth, widow of the Rev. Dr James Crombie, mother of Orr’s friend William Crombie.
7 William Sinclaire (1758-1807), linen merchant of Belfast and former United Irishman.
8 Probably William Seed, flour miller of Belfast.
9 Dr Alexander Haliday (1728-1802), physician, a leading citizen of Belfast (DNB).
10 Martha’ friend, Mrs Anne Orr, formerly matron of the Dublin Lying-in Hospital.
11 Mrs Ann Drennan (c.1719-1806).
12 John Kennedy (d. 1802), of Cultra, Co. Down (LG, p. 366); Bangor is a small port a few miles east of
Cultra, near the mouth of Belfast Lough.
13 Robert Stewart (1769-1822), Viscount Castlereagh, statesman (DNB); his wife, whom he married in 1794,
was Lady Emily Hobart (d. 1829), daughter of the 2nd Earl of Buckinghamshire.
14 Florida, Co. Down, was the home of David Gordon (1759-1837), attorney and later banker.
